title: Coding has become the easy part?
author: pikuray
selftext:
I have been working on my first AI project ever. It is an RPG game. I chose that because it's one of my favorite genre so it makes sense. 

But possibly the worst genre to make your first game in because RPG are more about feel than data. It's a lot of graphics, sounds, writing, worldbuilding. There's just so much many little things i took for granted. I think any adventure game is one of the most difficult thing you could do with AI because of that.

I think... Coding has become the easy and fun part???

I think i will keep working on my RPG on the backburner but i have to sacrifice the level of detail to something very simple-looking to finish in any reasonable time. 

I think as a beginner i should start with smaller scope games that don't require a lot of assets, like puzzle games, spreadsheet games, dating sims.

comments.author: wiggle_room1337
comments.body: the first 90% was always easy.  It's the second 90% that gets you.

comments.author: LiquidZebra
comments.body:
Just a heads up, I built a prototype Alpha of a tactical  RPG, new mechanics, and everything.

The thing they don’t tell you is that as you iterate to develop these systems, your code goes to shit. It’s easy to make, but the architecture of vibecoded “rpg” is beyond bad.

I just had to scrape a component that that I want to  
Migrate to a new repo from 4 different places. And I still missed 3 sources. 

Vibe coded RPG will get you to be able to showcase something rather quickly. If you are copying something, like D&D 5.x SRD, it’s better. If you are making a new system, it will hit a plateau and you will have to extract and migrate or rewrite.

Plus all the workflows need to be set up, like don’t put tasks and scratch into source control, or you will end up with a 9Gb repo for a 2D game

comments.author: Kindly-Sail6260
comments.body:
I was literally about to say the foundation for an rpg is the data itself. Everything else is just what makes it fun. 

My advice to OP would be to start on those smaller games. If you’re working on making an RPG, break down those systems into small games you can create. Idk if you’re going for a traditional western rpg or a jrpg, but either way you can start with whatever system that should be easy to make to help you understand all of the systems that go into making a fun rpg. 

I’ll give you some examples. 

You can start with combat. A small arena survivor where you can learn how enemies work or a dungeon crawler where it’s a simple find the exit and fight monsters along the way. Bonus points if you add locked doors and keys. You’ll learn level design, combat, enemy AI in one small game. 

Once you’ve completed that and it feels really good to play, then add chests, items and inventory management. You’ll learn what and how rewards feel when you find them, item rarity and balancing, and the kind of inventory system you want for your game. 

After that’s done, you can add a merchant system in your dungeon crawler. They can literally chill inside your dungeon randomly, which means that you’ll learn to create safe areas and use procedural generation to make the dungeon either bigger or have levels to them. That way you learn game economy and trading for better items as well as balancing buying and selling items. 

See the pattern? We can keep going all day, but if you follow everything in steps in one single game, you’ll realize that you created a small rpg by simply taking steps towards it. 

Most people won’t do this since traditional devs have to start smaller than this with games that they don’t want to make, but AI devs—I believe—will have a much better time learning how to make their dream game by breaking everything down into making a smaller version of the game they want to make. 

Good luck!

replies.author: COLES-BRAND-NUTMEG
replies.body:
Great advice. Doing one segment at a time gives you time to come to grips with them. When you introduce a second element the emergent variance is much easier to control.

Everything at once leaves you with a game you barely understand.

replies.author: Kindly-Sail6260
replies.body: It also allows you to separate systems too since AI can and will try to lump everything together.

comments.author: House13Games
comments.body: Its easy to get to a pretty prototype. It's orders of magnitude more difficult to make that into something people want to pay for.

comments.author: New_Internal5636
comments.body: Would say it always has been. The hard part is designing a good game that people want to play. Programming is only the hard part for noobs.

comments.author: Funny_Business_151
comments.body:
I can't code at all, so for me the code was never the hard part, Claude writes all of it. I started with a small dungeon crawler in the browser, find the exit and fight what's in the way, and added one thing at a time. It's on version 41 now.

What turned out hard was knowing if it's any fun. I thought it was fine until someone played it for a long time and told me it was too easy. I also built a whole town for it and later deleted it because it was a burden to go back to and took away from the main game.

So I'd say start small like you plan to, and get someone else to play it early. That told me more than anything I added myself.

replies.author: cutextwinklexcool
replies.body: Dating sims looked small to me too, until I counted the writing. Every choice needs a reaction, and every reaction has to make sense for that one person.

comments.body: Yea it was explained to me that rpgs were the least rewarding cause the player only experiences something one time like a boss or a cutscene.

comments.author: Aether_Ash_Forge
comments.body: I ended up putting my RPG on the back burner too and decided on a merge-puzzle alchemy game.

comments.author: HECRETSECRET
comments.body:
You should do the thing that gets you hyped. 

But yes coding is, relatively, the easy part. Rather prototyping is and thats what most early AI games are. A polished game is a marriage of art and code that takes you into the world of the game. All the graphical assets that are needed cannot come from the void and the ones that are online are basically assets you need pay for but a million people have done.

comments.author: ContDev
comments.body: yeah kinda felt the same with my first mobile game in unity, the code side moved way faster than i expected and the feel/polish stuff is where it slowed down lol. going smaller first sounds smart tbh, you'll actually ship something and learn the whole pipeline before going back to the rpg

comments.author: VortexAssetStudio
comments.body: 100% agree on rpgs being the hardest genre to finish solo. the code for an inventory or combat loop takes a weekend, then you realize you need hundreds of consistent icons, items, weapons, and ui elements just to make the world feel alive.honestly, instead of sacrificing visual detail or burning weeks trying to generate every single item one by one, the best move for an rpg is grabbing pre-made 2d asset packs for all the inventory/item clutter and saving your energy for the main characters and core gameplay. keeps the visual quality high without killing your momentum.
